open-question.question: Does the waiting wording live in the existing ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY slot, whose values already say how returns are handled as they land, or in a new slot of its own, with the concurrency slot left to say only how many dispatches run at once?
open-question.alternative: The waiting wording goes into the existing ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY slot, which keeps its name and its place at the opening of step 3. Each host's value is rewritten as one paragraph covering how many dispatches run at once, whether the run waits once for every return or batches each time it wakes, and, in the Codex value, when each agent is closed and the next question dispatched. No new slot is declared. ALTERNATIVES_DISPATCH, ALTERNATIVES_PROMPT_INSTRUCTIONS, ALTERNATIVES_AGENT, and AGENT_TOOL stay as they are, and each settings.toml comment for the slot is reworded to say it also governs how returns are collected. No new slot has to be declared in three settings.toml files and pass the slot-declaration check. The waiting sentence fills the one host-varying paragraph that already says how returns are handled as they land. The Codex rule that closes an agent only after its pipeline has finished, then dispatches the next pending question, stays in the same paragraph as the batching it now depends on, so the two cannot drift apart. Each value now mixes two concerns, how many agents are in flight and when returns are collected, so the slot's name and comment no longer describe all of it. Every host's value changes even where only the waiting half differs, so giving Antigravity or Codex a different waiting form than Claude Code means rewriting the whole concurrency paragraph for that host. How much the Codex value grows depends on the axis the Codex wait form question owns.

A new slot of its own (for example ALTERNATIVES_WAIT) holds only the waiting sentence. Hosts with a blocking wait get the wait-once-then-batch form, and a host without one gets the batch-per-wake-up form. All three hosts declare it, and it is used once in core/skills/provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions/SKILL.md as its own paragraph where the batch pipeline opens. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY is cut back to how many dispatches run at once (all together, or the Codex thread cap with close-and-refill) and drops its "as it lands" wording. The other three alternatives slots are unchanged. Each slot holds one concern, and the waiting sentence becomes exactly the one host slot the goal describes, with the per-wake-up form as one of its values. A host's waiting form can then change, for example Antigravity or Codex moving between the single-wait and per-wake-up forms, without touching its concurrency wording. A fourth alternatives slot has to be declared identically across three settings.toml files and used in core/, and the concurrency values still change because their "as it lands" wording must go. Codex's close-and-refill rule depends on when a question's batch has finished, so its two slot values have to be read together and can drift apart in a later edit, depending on the axis the Codex wait form question owns.

The waiting sentence is appended to the existing ALTERNATIVES_DISPATCH slot, which already names each host's agent tool (the Agent tool, spawn_agent). The wait sits beside the dispatch call as part of that host's tool-specific mechanics. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY keeps its count wording minus "as it lands". No new slot is declared. Each host's tool names sit in one value: the dispatch tool and the tool or loop it waits with. A reader of one host's settings.toml finds the whole dispatch-and-collect mechanism in one place, again without declaring a new slot. That slot ends where the dispatch prompt's fenced block opens, so the waiting sentence would come before the prompt whose returns it waits for, and its comment would have to be redefined. It mixes run control with the description of what the prompt carries, which the re-dispatch repair reuses as "the same prompt". The concurrency wording also still has to change, so the change touches two slots anyway.

No slot carries the waiting wording. Shared prose in core/ states it as a capability test that the runner applies at run time: where the host offers a blocking wait, wait once and batch; where it does not, batch at each wake-up. This mirrors the "where the host can run several agent dispatches at once" phrasing already inside the concurrency values. ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY drops its "as it lands" wording and otherwise keeps its count wording. No slot is added or widened. No host has to be classified at build time. Antigravity, whose return delivery the repository does not record, and Codex, with no waiting tool named anywhere, each fall into the right branch by what the runner actually finds. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees stay byte-identical without assuming either host has a wait. It rejects the goal's own statement that the waiting sentence is the one host slot, so it needs a goal revision first. It also leaves to the runner's judgment during each run a choice that build-time slot values would otherwise settle for good. Whether it is still worth doing depends on the axes the Codex wait form and Antigravity wait form questions own.

open-question.question: What does the orchestrator do when the blocking wait ends before every dispatched agent has finished: embed and commit what has landed and wait again, fall back to per-wake-up batching for the rest, or treat the unfinished agents as skipped?
open-question.alternative: When the blocking wait ends with agents still unfinished, the orchestrator pipes every file that has landed so far into one `embed --alternatives` batch and commits each question that embedded, in one shell call. It then issues the same blocking wait again for the agents still outstanding, and repeats until every dispatched agent has landed a file or ended in a failure. No limit is set on how many times it waits again, nothing is skipped because of an expiry, and the run keeps the single-wait form throughout. Finished work is committed at every expiry, so a slow agent never holds the rest hostage and an interrupted run loses only uncommitted returns. Each expiry adds just one batch-plus-wait turn pair, and the run stays in one waiting form on one host. A hung agent keeps the run waiting forever unless the wait's completion test turns it into a failure some other way (the sibling "Wait completion and failure test" owns that). A run with several expiries also makes several batch calls, so the goal's "wakes once per run" holds only when nothing expires.

alternative.id: Embed landed, wait bounded times, then skip

open-question.alternative: At each expiry the orchestrator embeds and commits every landed file in one shell call, then waits again for the outstanding agents. It does this up to a fixed number of further waits (or a fixed total waiting time). After the last allowed wait it embeds whatever has landed and treats every agent still unfinished as skipped. Those questions are listed in the step-4 still-skipped advisory, and a later run of the pass picks them up because their blocks still carry no alternatives. The run's length is bounded, so a hung or runaway agent cannot stall the pass, and slow but healthy agents still get several chances to land. Committed progress accumulates at every expiry. It adds a tunable bound (a count or a duration) to the prose, and that bound has to be justified per host. An agent skipped at the bound may still finish later and write a file that nothing embeds, wasting its tokens and leaving an orphan in the scratch directory. It also stretches the skip from "refused after repair" to "too slow", which changes what the advisory means.

alternative.id: Hold landed, wait again until all land

open-question.alternative: At an expiry the orchestrator embeds nothing. It just issues the blocking wait again for the outstanding agents, with no limit, so every landed file stays in the scratch directory until the whole set has landed or failed. Then it embeds and commits the whole set in the one batch shell call the goal describes. An expiry is invisible to the batching: the run still makes exactly one embed-and-commit call. It keeps the goal's single-wake, single-batch shape exactly, whatever the host's wait cap. The orchestrator adds no branch, only a repeated wait, which is the smallest change to the waiting sentence. Nothing is committed until the slowest agent finishes, so an orchestrator that dies or is interrupted mid-wait commits none of the landed work, and a re-run re-dispatches every bare block. A hung agent stalls the whole run unless the wait's completion test (owned by the sibling "Wait completion and failure test") ends it some other way.

alternative.id: Hold landed, wait bounded times, then batch and skip

open-question.alternative: At an expiry the orchestrator embeds nothing and waits again, up to a fixed number of further waits (or a fixed total waiting time). When every agent has landed or failed, or the bound is reached, it embeds and commits every landed file in one batch shell call. Any agent still unfinished at the bound is treated as skipped and reported in the step-4 still-skipped advisory, to be picked up by a later run of the pass. It keeps exactly one embed-and-commit call per run and still bounds how long the run can last, so neither a long wait cap nor a hung agent changes the batch shape or stalls the pass forever. Landed work stays uncommitted for the whole bounded window, so an interruption loses all of it. It adds a tunable bound, and skipping slow agents leaves orphan files and wasted agent tokens just as the progressive bounded form does.

alternative.id: Embed landed, switch to per-wake-up batching

open-question.alternative: At the first expiry the orchestrator embeds and commits every landed file in one shell call. It then drops the blocking wait for the rest of the run and handles the outstanding agents the way a host without a blocking wait does: it batches every landed return each time it wakes on the host's own completion signal, until every agent has landed or failed. The single-wait form covers the first window, and the per-wake-up form covers whatever is left after it. It reuses the per-wake-up path the goal already writes for hosts without a blocking wait, so expiry needs no new waiting logic. The orchestrator stops blocking on a tool call it cannot extend, and slow agents are still embedded as they finish. Both waiting forms have to be live and correct on the same host within one run, so the waiting sentence must describe the hand-off between them. It works only where the host also delivers per-agent completion wake-ups, which depends on which primitive the sibling "Claude Code wait primitive" picks and on what the siblings "Codex wait form" and "Antigravity wait form" settle. After the switch the run returns to several wake-ups, some of them turns that do nothing.

When the wait ends early, the orchestrator embeds and commits every landed file in one shell call and treats every agent still unfinished as skipped. It neither waits again nor switches form. The skipped questions are listed in the step-4 still-skipped advisory, and their blocks stay bare, so the next run of the pass dispatches them afresh. It is the simplest rule and keeps the run to exactly one wait and one batch, with a hard ceiling on run time set by the host's wait cap. Recovery is already built in, because the pass's idempotent gather re-selects every bare block on its next run. Any agent slower than one wait cap loses its work every time, so on a host with a short cap (a ten-minute foreground call) a large or slow question can be skipped run after run. Agents still running write files that no one embeds, wasting their tokens, unless the orchestrator also stops them. It also turns "slow" into a skip reason that the existing one-repair-then-skip contract never had.

open-question.question: Does the Antigravity tree carry the same waiting sentence as Claude Code, keeping the two trees byte-identical on the assumption that it offers the same wait, or the per-wake-up value, given that the repository records nothing about how Antigravity delivers agent returns?
open-question.alternative: Claude Code and Antigravity both get one identical slot value that names both forms by capability instead of naming one form. Where the runner can block in one call until every dispatched agent's return has landed or failed, it names the scratch directory, waits once, and batches the whole set. Otherwise it batches every time it wakes with landed returns. The two trees stay byte-identical, and on Antigravity the runner decides at run time which form applies. It keeps the byte-identity end-to-end test and still never commits Antigravity to a wait it may lack. It follows the existing ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY wording ("where the host can … and … where it cannot") and the rule that host-dependent sentences name the capability, never the host. It needs no evidence about Antigravity to be correct. The Claude Code sentence becomes less direct. Every run, the runner has to judge its own capability, and on Claude Code it could fall back to per-wake-up batching and lose the saving the milestone is for. It also blurs the goal's design of a slot carrying one form per host, with per-wake-up as the value for a host without a wait. On Antigravity the wait branch still covers only hosts whose wait matches the primitive the Claude Code wording describes, which the "Claude Code wait primitive" sibling decides.

The Antigravity definition's waiting slot gets exactly the Claude Code value: the single-wait form, in which the orchestrator names the run's scratch directory, waits in one call until every dispatched agent's return has landed or failed, then embeds and commits the whole set in one shell call. The Claude Code and Antigravity trees stay byte-identical apart from the plugin-root literal and the stripped `color` key. Antigravity is assumed to offer the same wait, and nothing is probed or recorded about how it actually delivers agent returns. It keeps the Claude Code / Antigravity byte-identity, which CLAUDE.md names as the slot mechanism's only end-to-end test, since no pytest covers it. It also follows the precedent already set: the Antigravity tree's ALTERNATIVES_DISPATCH, AGENT_TOOL, and ALTERNATIVES_CONCURRENCY values already copy Claude Code's `Agent` tool and `cairn:` registry wording without host-specific evidence. No unverified Antigravity-specific value gets authored, and the CLAUDE.md invariant needs no change. It rests on an untested assumption. The repository records nothing about whether Antigravity dispatches agents in the background or offers a blocking wait, and `docs/skill-reference.md` already records one way it differs: it has no session continuation. If the wait is missing, the Antigravity orchestrator follows an instruction it cannot carry out, and it may hang until a cap, misread an unfinished run, or skip questions. How much this matters depends on which primitive the Claude Code sentence names (owned by the "Claude Code wait primitive" sibling). A shell loop polling the scratch directory carries over to any host with a shell more readily than a host-specific notification tool does.

The Antigravity definition's waiting slot gets the per-wake-up form, the value the goal defines for a host without a blocking wait: the orchestrator embeds and commits in a batch every time it wakes with landed returns. Claude Code keeps the single-wait form. On this one slot the Antigravity tree stops being byte-identical to the Claude Code tree. It is the safe value for a host whose behaviour is unknown. Per-wake-up batching is correct whether Antigravity delivers returns one at a time (where it falls back to the old per-return cadence), in groups, or all at once after blocking dispatches. It never asks the orchestrator for a wait that may not exist, so the worst case is lost savings, never a hung or misjudged run. It ends the Claude Code / Antigravity byte-identity that CLAUDE.md names as the slot mechanism's end-to-end test, and the invariant's wording has to be revised. If Antigravity does offer a blocking wait, it gives up the single wake-up per run on that host. The Antigravity value is also chosen without evidence, just in the cautious direction.

Before the Antigravity slot value is fixed, this milestone runs a probe on the locally installed `agy` CLI. A headless `agy -p` run of the alternatives pass on a scratch milestone observes whether agent dispatches run in the background, how their completions reach the orchestrator, and whether one call can block until every return has landed. The slot then gets the single-wait value if the probe shows a usable blocking wait and the per-wake-up value otherwise. The finding goes into the milestone's starting state, so the repository records it from then on. The value is set on evidence rather than assumption, in either direction. The repository gains its first recorded knowledge of how Antigravity delivers agent returns, and that knowledge also informs the existing repair branch and future host slots. The `agy` binary is already installed on the maintainer's machine, so the probe needs no new setup. It adds a probe task and leaves the slot value open until the probe runs. Headless print mode may not show everything an interactive session would. The finding holds for one `agy` version and can go stale without notice, because no test or CI run exercises Antigravity. It also involves running a real alternatives pass, with commits, against a throwaway milestone.

open-question.question: What does the orchestrator do with a question whose agent ended with DONE but whose file is absent from the scratch directory when the batch scans: treat it as a refused return and send its one repair, skip it and list it in the still-skipped advisory, or leave its block bare with no report for the next run of the pass to re-dispatch?

In the per-wake-up form, where a batch scan can run while another agent is still writing its file, how is a partially written file kept out of embed: the agent writes under a temporary name and renames once the file is complete, the scan pipes only files whose agent has already ended, or the risk is accepted and a refused partial return is handled as any other refusal?

Where the single wait is the dispatch call's own blocking form, how does the orchestrator wait for a repaired return sent as a continuation message to the held agent session, which is not a dispatch: the continuation is sent in the same blocking form, repairs are re-dispatched fresh so the blocking form applies, or repaired returns fall to per-wake-up batching?

On a host that dispatches in cap-sized rounds, does a round's repair set get its own wait-and-batch before the next round is dispatched, or do the repairs ride in the next round's wait beside that round's first dispatches, counting against the cap?

What does the one batch shell call print so the orchestrator can tell which questions embed refused and with which Error line, given that embed prints nothing on success and the call pipes several files: each file's Short Title ahead of its embed output, only the refused titles each paired with its Error line, or nothing beyond the tool's own stderr?
